utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First of all, let me indicate that unfortunately Judge Orie is not with us today for urgent personal matters. Judge Fluegge and I have decided that it is in the interests of justice to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis, as we now do. The Chamber is informed that both parties have preliminary issues to raise, starting with the Prosecution. Yes, Madam Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And thank you. Your Honour, in an abundance of caution I would ask to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We haven't finished dealing with the associated exhibits with Mr. Kralj, so I don't want -- I don't know if Your Honours want to deal with it now or we should wait for Judge Orie or for Monday, whatever you instruct us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suggest we wait for Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then that is all?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May the witness please be brought into the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration that you have made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Harbour, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's your chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, yesterday you told the Court that your Muslim colleagues, Drs. Torlak and Berberkic were detained in in KP Dom. Did you know that another doctor from your hospital, Dr. Asima Pilav, was also detained in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Asima Pilav was detained at the beginning of the war in Velecevo, not at the KP Dom, Velecevo. It's an infirmary; at the beginning of the war, it was a prison. Dr. Asima Pilav was a paediatrician.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Doctors and medical staff who worked at the Foca health centre, including Dr. Karovic, were also transferred to KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Ibro Karovic is a doctor from the medical centre; he was at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: After the health centre staff were arrested and detained, did you and the remaining doctors at the Foca hospital make an appeal on the radio for a release of all the doctors?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection: Assumes facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I -- I am not sure which facts are being assumed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you point to where there has been evidence led of an arrest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does it have to be in evidence? It's the position of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then she has to preface it by saying it's the position of the Prosecutor - does she not? - if she is presenting the Prosecution's position on something? We have not had evidence led that these individuals were arrested at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you understand that Madam Harbour is on cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what are the limitations on cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is a limitation that if you assume a fact not in evidence, it's subject to objection unless you are presenting your case pursuant to the rule, in which case you have to identify it as being your position.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would be happy to rephrase the question if that would cut to the chase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: After the health centre staff were detained at KP Dom, did you and the other remaining doctors at the Foca hospital make an appeal on the radio for the release of all the doctors?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 27536 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just let me find out: What's the difference between this question and the previous question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: As I understand Mr. Ivetic's objection, the previous question I had said "arrested and detained," whereas, as rephrased, I omitted the word "arrested."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, yesterday at transcript page 27536 you testified that after the 8th of April, 1992, specialists, including Muslim doctors, "abandoned" the hospital due to the conflict. In paragraph 5 of your statement when you discussed Muslim staff leaving the hospital, you said "no one drove them out." This is not exactly accurate, is it, considering that Muslim doctors and medical staff were detained in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the conflict certainly caused fear amongst everyone regardless of ethnicity. People were trying to resolve their own situations. They didn't want to have the conflict affect them entirely. Yesterday I stated it wasn't only the Muslim doctors at the hospital but the Serb doctors, too, out of fear left the hospital, their patients, seeking to find a solution for themselves and their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you mind if I just ask a question. Doctor, were any Serb doctors detained at the KP Dom or at any penitentiary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Foca?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Foca, I don't know -- not in Foca as far as I know. In other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't speculate. Thank you so much. You may proceed, Madam Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 31524 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And, Dr. Maric, this is a map of the area around Foca town that identifies various places that are relevant to this case. These places include the health centre, KP Dom, and the hospital. So once we have the map on the screen -- can you understand the English markings?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Okay. In that case I will go through them. At the very top of the map, the marking points to the hospital. Can you verify that this is where the hospital was located?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the right bank of the Drina. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Further down the next marking is "KP Dom." Can you verify that is the correct location?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: KP Dom, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now moving to the left along the Drina, we have the SUP; is that correct -- in the correct location?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Continuing down there is Partizan Hall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Turning towards the right now there is Aladza Mosque; is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the right bank of the Cehotina and here it's on the left. The Aladza Mosque is on the banks of the Cehotina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Okay. If we continue to the right, the health centre is marked; is that the location of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And finally the last marking is the high school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The high school is on the right bank of the Cehotina, not the left one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, bearing in mind the witness's testimony about the map, I would still like to tender this into evidence, given the place -- locations that he was able to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know -- I don't know how we're going to deal with the correction. I still don't know the source of the map, if the scale has been added by the Prosecution or if that's from the map itself. If the scale is with the map, that's fine; if it's been added by the Prosecution, then we need to know how they've derived it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, who put on the scale? It looks like it comes with the map, but I don't want to pre-empt your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am informed that our mapping unit includes this scale based on the side -- the scale of the original map. This was originally a topographical map of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was 1:25.000, so the mapping people derived this scale from that scale, the original map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness in relation to this map. Witness, you said the high school is on the right bank of the Cehotina River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you look at the map, it is indicated there that it is indeed on the right bank of the river, so there is no contradiction. It is the last marking on the top right -- in the lower right corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I saw these red markings, and I think that if the arrow is by the road, then what I said and what is written here is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then the marking is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said it was on the right bank of the Cehotina; that's where the high school is. So I didn't see the Aladza Mosque and the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you agree with almost all markings except the Aladza Mosque; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The mistakes have been reduced by 50 per cent. What is Defence's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They are, Your Honour. And as long as we are not then going to rely upon the markings as being authoritative, they can be demonstrative of approximate locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. We appreciate it. Then the map then would be -- did you ask for it to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P6866.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. P6866. You may proceed, Madam Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this Chamber has heard evidence that Muslim prisoners in KP Dom were kept in poor conditions, that they were freezing, that they were underfed, that they were physically beaten, that there were Muslims who were very sick, who suffered serious heart problems, or who were mentally ill while they were detained in KP Dom, and some people, especially elderly people, died as a result of these poor conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: This is, for Your Honours, from Exhibit P738, pages 7 to 8, which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, you have made some assertions in paragraphs 19 and 20 of your statement. You've stated that as far as you knew there was no discrimination in the treatment of KP Dom detainees, that military and civilian authorities had no influence over the doctors, and that detainees went to the hospital when that was necessary. Now, you do not have actual knowledge of the health conditions of the detainees in KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KP Dom is a separate institution. It takes care of everything including the health care for its clients, so I'm not familiar with the situation but I know that patients before the conflict and during the conflict -- I mean patients from the KP Dom. And to this day since they do not have comprehensive medical care, they are sent to the hospital when necessary. And even during the conflict those who came to the hospital were also operated on. Now what the situation is, I would not be a relevant person to say what their situation was because I wasn't up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does it mean, then, Doctor, that when you are alleged to have said that so far as you knew there was no discrimination in the treatment of KP Dom detainees, you were not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in the context because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to explain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just asking: You were not correct; is that correct? Because you have just told us you don't know the conditions in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, doctors from the hospital who helped and who went up there during the conflict, they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shall I stop you there? Shall I stop you there? You have said two statements which are inconsistent. You have said in your statement that people in the KP Dom were not discriminated against. Now you are saying the KP Dom was a separate institution, you have no knowledge of the conditions there; therefore, when you said that people were not discriminated in the KP Dom, you were not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, ignoring the evidence that he's testified about detainees coming to be treated as patients in the hospital, of which he was involved in, and that's the evidence that was right after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Detainees in the hospital are detainees in the hospital. I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, detainees -- Your Honour, detainees from KP Dom to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From KP -- I accept that. Detainees from KP Dom to the hospital are detained -- I'm talking about detainees in the KP Dom, not who were taken to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The detainees from KP Dom are taken to the hospital; they are still detainees of KP Dom, Your Honour. So I think Your Honour's assertion that his statement is incorrect is not entirely in line with the evidence that has been led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me quote to you what Madam Harbour quoted and which you didn't object to. Now, if you look at page 11 from line 19, Madam Harbour quotes paragraph 19 of the accused [sic] and 20 and she says: "You have stated that as far as you knew there was no discrimination in the treatment of KP Dom detainees ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the treatment of KP Dom detainees. If you look at temporary transcript page 12, lines 1 through 4, the witness says that: "... KP Dom is a separate institution. It takes care of everything including the health care for its clients, so I'm not familiar with the situation but I know that patients before the conflict and during the conflict, I mean patients from the KP Dom and to this day, since they do not have comprehensive medical care they are sent to the hospital when necessary. And even during the conflict, those who came to the hospital were also operated on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's in line with his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He's speaking about patients. We don't know about what was done to those detainees who were not patients, so he can't talk about the treatment of detainees at the KP Dom; he can talk about the patients who came from the KP Dom who -- for his treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, when he's talking about treatment as a doctor, there is only one type of treatment, that's medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I overrule your objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] Please proceed, Madam Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic now, Dr. Maric. Yesterday at transcript page 27554, you said that during April 1992 you treated 48 patients surgically and 37 of those patients were Muslim. I would like to ask you about a number of the wounded people from Foca who were treated at your hospital during this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: So if we could please have 65 ter 1D04416 and page 24 in the English, page 12 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: As this is coming up, just for your reference, this is the patients admission log that you've referred to in a few paragraphs in your statement. Here at number 2663, we have Mensur Borovina, born in 1982; and then number 2664 is Mohammed Softic, born in 1989. In the diagnosis column we see variations of vulnera sclopetaria for both. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because on the right-hand side one page is missing. It's a book with two pages, one of each side and the right-hand side page is missing. That's why I can't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now do you see the column, the diagnosis column?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can remove the English version and look at the B/C/S version and that can be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you for the suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, these diagnoses of, again, Mensur Borovina and Mohammed Softic indicate injuries due to firearms; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Can you confirm that these entries reflect that Muslim children, approximately 10 and 3 years old, had been shot?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be an expert on that. I can just tell you that this is a diagnosis, vulnera sclopetarium, and that those who suffered those wounds were young patients, children. Softic was a child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said 10 and 3 years old. What do you mean by that? If we look at the entry 2663, the date of birth should be 1982. And what about the other one, born in 1962?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you are referring to the next one?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, can you confirm that these were Muslims, Muslim children? Could you please state your answer verbally?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we turn now to page 12 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S. Or if Your Honours are comfortable, we could just stick with the B/C/S, it may be easier for the witness to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you propose.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In that case page 6 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Here at number 2605, we see Halim Dzalilovic [phoen], born in 1929 from Codor Mahala in Foca, diagnosis vulnus sclopetarium. Further down at 2609 we see Hamdija Hadzimuratovic, born in 1923, same diagnosis. These entries reflect that Muslims in their 60s also had fire-arm injuries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct but war and arms did not make a distinction between young and old. A total of 2.500 people were wounded in Foca during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we now turn to page 14 in the English -- or, actually, we'll just turn to page 7 in the B/C/S and we'll focus on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At item 2615 we have Ismeta Hodzic, daughter of Dzemal, worker in a sock factory, same diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And then if we could turn to page 10 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want any comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Deal with them as a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: -- deal with both of these at the same --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We see at number 2648 further down, Jasmina Sirbubalo, same diagnosis. From these entries we see that Muslim women were also admitted after receiving fire-arms injuries in April 1992; is that correct, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, yes. But I told you what happened: 2500 people were wounded. I myself treated 2500 Serbs. I operated on them. There were also people of other ethnicities. I treated them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, if you could just answer my questions we would -- that would be much appreciated. Now, you said in paragraph 5 of your statement that the conflicts forced people to "go where their own people were." Did incidents of women, children, and the elderly being shot contribute to Foca's Muslims moving to where their own people were, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts in Foca lasted for perhaps 10 days or a fortnight. I can't remember exactly. And it is in turn that as a result there was a lot fear, a lot of people wounded, and people dealt with that situation as best as they could. Some 500 to 800 of them stayed at the hospital at first and they were of all ethnicities, and after that --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Do you agree with me that these incidents contributed to Muslims moving to where their own people were, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Separated families decided to unite where they felt the safest, and that would be my answer. And they felt the safest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I stop you, Doctor. Can I suggest that you please listen carefully to the question, and we are not asking you to justify --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- or explain why things happened. You are just being asked to say why things happened or didn't happen. The question is simply: Do you agree that these shootings contributed to the Muslims going to their own people? I suppose they might have contributed to the Serbs going to their own people?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, he has answered the question. He answered the question with the first answer of that answer. So what's the objection? What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He said "of course." He said "of course." That's an answer, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, and then he went on to explain, which I said please --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he has answered the question. You're implying that he has not answered the question. He listened to the question, he answered the question. I fail to see the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you should calm down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- I agree, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It will help you if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would like to talk to you now about a few of the Muslim children which are on the paediatric ward admission list which you have also discussed in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 1D4415, and if we -- if Your Honours don't mind, I will continue to only show the B/C/S. So that's page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In rows 154 and 155 we see Selma and Jasenko Tafro born in 1984 and 1985, so they were around 7 and 8 years old, and we see there is no diagnosis for them. In the diagnosis column it simply says "moved to ophthalmology ward." Do you know why these two children ended up in Foca hospital?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But the hospital was open to everybody who knocked on the door. We accommodated the children where we had room for them and then they left on the 25th of September, both of them, when we found a way to place them with their families. I don't know when they were admitted as a matter of fact. They were admitted on the 28th of August, which means that they spent about a month in the hospital. They were not with the sick and the wounded, but we looked after them. They did not have to be physically sick. We still looked after them because they were under a lot stress and they had nowhere to go, so both these children spent about a month with us before we were able to find them a place to go to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 31521, page 3 in the English and there is only the one page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You may be familiar with Janko Janjic, also known as Tuta. He was indicted at this Tribunal for crimes that he committed against Muslims in Foca as part of a unit under Brane Cosovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And I also refer Your Honours to Exhibit P979, paragraph 68, which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: This article from the 14th of September, 1994, states in the last paragraph in the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S it's on the far right column, the second paragraph. So maybe that can be enlarged for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Here it states: "Tuta and his accomplices first raped the mother of the 8-year-old Jasko and his slightly older sister Selma Tafro and then killed her and her husband Tafro in front of her neighbours and the aforementioned children in Samoborska Street in the centre of town."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where can we find it in the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: That is at the bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Maric, you said that these children were under a lot stress and they had nowhere to go. Isn't it true that they were taken to the hospital because their parents were killed and there was nowhere else to send them?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On admission into every health care institution, a reason has to be stated for admission. I'm a surgeon. I don't know anything about the admission procedure. Those children were admitted and they were looked after for a month. I'm a surgeon. I work in the operating room. I don't know why those children were admitted. I know that these children spent a month at the eye department. Not only the two of them, there were other children who shared their fate and they were in the same situation. So that's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that there were other children who shared their fate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we could go back to 65 ter 1D4415, page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you just about two more of these children.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Your Honours, could I tender this article into evidence? It's 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that 31521?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see no objection. Yes, Mr. Registrar, its admitted, may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit P6867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Madam Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: On this page just above the Tafro siblings, we see in row 153 Azra Ramovic, born in 1988. And again, it simply states that she was moved to the ophthalmology ward. Yesterday at transcript page 27547, you identified Azra as one of the children who was taken to Igalo after 1993.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Further down on the same page we see in row 160 Kemal, and if you can make out his surname it seems to be Soro, born in 1988, also sent to the ophthalmology ward?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soro.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Soro.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Born?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Do you know why Azra and Kemal were at Foca hospital?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Azra Ramovic spent anything between a year and then three years with a group of the seven children that I sent to Igalo. When children are cured and when we don't have anywhere to send them, we put them at other departments. They don't have to stay at children -- so she was also at the eye department until 1993 when she was taken to Igalo. Don't think that the fact that children are moved from one department to another in the hospital that it is something strange. First, they are treated at the child disease department and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you speak too fast, they can't -- they are not able to keep up with you, so speak slowly. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this young boy Soro, he was discharged on the 25th of September, 1992. I can't see the date of admission, but I suppose that -- I don't know. This seems to be April 04. I can't see that. He was not wounded. He was not sick. That's why he was kept at the department for eye diseases. It was a large department. The -- there were few patients. The eye disease department is for eye diseases, but I don't want you to be confused about the fact that we kept children there. There was nowhere else to keep them. Once they were treated and they were cured and when there was no other department to go to, we would move them to the eye diseases department.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's understood. We have a statement from Kemal Soro.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 31519, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: As this is coming up, I will just summarise for you what the statement says. He says on page 2 that one days Serb soldiers attacked his house in the area of Foca called Codor Mahala. His father and his uncle were taken to KP Dom. On page 3 he says he moved to his grandparents house.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And if we could now go to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Kemal said that Serb soldiers attacked his grandparents' house as well. He hid in the tree while Serb soldiers set fire to the house and fired shots. The next morning Kemal went to the house of a Serb neighbour. The Serb neighbour directed him to the hospital. Kemal did not know what happened to his grandfather, to his uncle, two aunts and their children who had been at his grandfather's house. He was placed at the hospital in a room with only Muslim children. Azra, who was 3 years old, was one of the children there. She had been staying with Kemal's mother and she told Kemal that Serb soldiers had come into the house, had lined up everyone, had shot at their legs, and this 3-year-old had wounds all over her legs. Kemal's mother and brother were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I have a reference for "Serb soldiers"; it's not in the statement. If I can help, it only says "soldiers." If you rephrase your question, we will remove the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the middle of paragraph 3, I see there: "The female neighbour told me that she was worried that the Serb soldiers would come to her house and do the same things to them and kill them."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: End quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you appreciate that it's two different incidents we're talking about. She's talking about the next paragraph, which is a different incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just quoted from the statement, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, soldiers. Azra was telling Kemal about an incident when soldiers came into her house, lined up everyone in the house, shot at their legs. She was 3 years old. She had wounds all over her legs and Kemal's mother and brother were killed. And is it correct, Dr. Maric, that like the Tafro siblings, Kemal and Azra were at Foca hospital because their families were killed and there was nowhere else to send them?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only place -- actually, the boy could not be sent from the place where he was to the hospital on his own. Somebody had to bring him because he was 3 kilometres away. Why they were brought to the hospital, I don't know. I told you already that I'm a surgeon and whoever sought medical attention was admitted. They could be admitted for sickness, injuries, or other conditions. And I was never on any patient's admission, so I can't answer your question as to why they were admitted. I'm just saying that the young boy had to be brought by somebody because the place from which he arrived was 3 kilometres away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: But you agree that Muslim children who were not wounded were held at the hospital for periods of time because there was not another place to send them? I think you've already given a -- you've already mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving you about the good thing. I'm telling you that even a hospital who was not originally tasked with that role still performed that role, irrespective of other legally prescribed duties. The hospital performed a humanitarian task as well. We were supposed to admit sick and wounded and treat them, but we did other things as well. Even today we have children --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in hospital whose parents don't want to look after them so we look after them, we bring them up, we try to find a place for them to live. So this is our humanitarian role as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much longer are you likely to be, Madam Harbour?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would probably take another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's much more than the 45 minutes you have indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'm not sure where we are on time now, but I think you are correct. If -- with your indulgence, I would seek an extra 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Try to be focused also in your questions. If the witness has already said something, there is no need to go back to it, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do so. In paragraph -- would -- should we take a break now a bit early or -- before I move into the next section, or should I continue for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you take more than three minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Maybe not. Let me finish this next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's finish it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of your statement, Dr. Maric, you stated that in 1992 you tried to hand children from other ethnic groups over to Muslim authorities, and you said the reason to this was: "Out of fear that a drunk or a madman would come to the hospital and harm those children." There is evidence in this case that armed guards took several Muslims from the hospital in late April and shot them outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And this is from P741, paragraph 4, which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Was this the kind of incident that made you fear that those children might be harmed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true. Nobody was taken out of the hospital or killed within the hospital's perimeter. There was a war and as a living being I was afraid and I was afflicted by other things as a result of the conflict, that's why I sympathised with all the people who survived the conflict in Bosnia that lasted from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please -- could we please have Exhibit 989 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And in moving into a different topic now. This is a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is a P number, 989?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness. Sir, the incident Ms. Harbour referred to, is it not true that this happened, that patients were taken out and killed during the war at any time? Are you saying that this never happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is that the hospital admitted people, treated them, and discharged them. If a person is discharged, well, they leave the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the question. The question is: If at any point in time during the war patients were taken out by other people, not by people of the hospital, and killed outside. Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I don't think that that could have ever happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least unbeknownst to me because I'm a man who was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: This -- if I could turn your attention now to the screen. This is a report dated the 12th of October, 1992. To --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 12th or 10th?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: 10th -- my apologies, 10th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Sent from Marko Kovac to the Herzegovina Corps. And in item number 3 it discusses an ICRC visit to the Foca hospital where they had private conversations with 21 Muslims, eight women, and two men.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We see that Kovac states under item 4: "We have 21 Muslim children and a number of women for exchange, or we would send them to Gorazde." Dr. Maric, you said that the hospital tried to hand children over to the Muslim authorities, was that so that they could be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't know what Kovac was saying. It's 1992 when I was not director of the hospital. But certainly a longer stay and then there is this interest, we were friends. Irrespective of ethnicity there were certainly links and we certainly wanted to help one another. That's what I spoke about. This exchange that Kovac is speaking about, I don't know. He probably came and took that number of patients and wrote to his superior command, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And just going back to your statement when you said that you tried to hand children over to the Muslim authorities. In your -- when you testified in Karadzic, you did say that you were involved in the exchange of some children for Serbs. Is that -- do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 Dzudo, who was there for two years, a little boy, and the daughter of a friend of ours, we tried to hand them over at Osanica; that's where the separation line was. We tried to hand them over to the other entity because their parents were there. We didn't manage the first time. We went back and then we tried again to hand them over because they were our friends. We tried to bring them to the line safely. I think that the little boy, Dzudo, was handed over, and Revko Prguda was handed over and then Dzudo when he celebrated his 20th birthday he came to the children's department at the hospital in Foca where he had spent so much time. So it wasn't an exchange. It was just what I tried to explain to you, that they were handed over to the other side, the Muslim side, where Gorazde was and the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you then try to answer the question that was put to you, Doctor. Your answer doesn't answer the question that was put to you. The question that was put to you was: Do you stand by the testimony that you gave in the Karadzic case that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- just listen to me -- that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- we are going to do testimony, I believe the procedure in this courtroom has also been to present the testimony if we are going to ask a witness to stand by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a different story. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, his -- what he has just described does comport with his Karadzic testimony and that would be at Karadzic transcript page 35606 to 35607, and where he talks about this exchange of this boy, Dzuderija. So if Your Honours are satisfied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. Does that round off your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honours, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it convenient to take a break right now?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break now -- and you will be -- can you be back in 20 minutes, Dr. Maric, that will be at five to 11.00. Thank you so much. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We adjourn and come back at five to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness, Your Honour, I again rise to clarify the record in relation to Your Honour's question at transcript page 12, line 10. Paragraph 19 of the witness's statement which is in evidence is as D730 does not relate to detainees at KP Dom but relates exclusively to the patients in the KPD as the witness testified in court so that that should hopefully clarify the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it is at least possible to understand it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the -- no discrimination in the treatment of patients in the KPD. That may relate to treatment -- no discrimination of treatments in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the disconnect is. I'm talking about patients as well in the KP Dom, not detainees that are not patients which was the -- Your Honour's question -- Your Honour's -- Judge Moloto's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It doesn't say "from KP Dom" but "in KP Dom."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So -- and therefore it is understandable to understand it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To relate to patients, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. What Judge Fluegge is saying it is also capable to say that people who are in the KP Dom treated the detainees in the KP Dom in a particular fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In it's related to patients. Your Honour's question was related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- persons that were not patients. It's specifically included --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the statement says "detainees," it doesn't say "patients."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says "patients" actually, Your Honour. That's why I'm rising to clarify that the statement only says "patients." It does not say "detainees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But "in the KP Dom." This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the problem. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is no problem there. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Harbour, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, in October 1993 Karadzic visited Foca hospital to celebrate the opening of the medical school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic and his wife visited the Foca hospital. A visit was organised to the Foca hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 31518B.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, the document I'm calling up is the transcript of a radio presentation covering Dr. Karadzic's visit to the hospital in 1993. The announcer states that this was Karadzic's first visit to Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 2 in the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We see that Karadzic said: "We had no problems in Foca, which is why we have not visited before." And then he ends his speech by saying: "It is important for the citizens of Foca to know that the Muslim republic has given up on Foca." The reporter then announces that Karadzic visited the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The reporter refers to Maksimovic, Petko Cancar, Dr. Veljko Maric, and Drina Tactical Group Commander Marko Kovac. One of these speakers indicated as US2 states that Karadzic could: "... see today with his own eyes that life in Foca is organised in a typical Serbian way ..." And he goes on to praise the functional civilian government, the secure front lines, the revived economy and education system.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And now if we could turn to page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The speaker US4, which is NG4 in B/C/S, says: "We shall continue as we have performed so far and President Radovan Karadzic will continue to be happy with our work. He has approved our plans and encouraged us in our sound medical thinking about the future and in general ..." And then in the last line: "... the Medical School must be the first faculty to open in our new state." Dr. Maric, you were NG4, the speaker who gave this last speech; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The next speaker was Marko Kovac, who said: "I am very happy that I had the honour today to be in the presence of our Supreme Commander." Several lines later, he says: "On behalf of the Serbian army, I am extremely grateful to our Supreme Commander who spent time with us today. I wish him to continue to lead us from one victory to another so we could as quickly as possible defend our Serbian Republic for which he deserves a lot credit." So during this event we have Karadzic saying we had no problems in Foca, followed by congratulatory speeches by various leaders and yourself, and concluding with Marko Kovac crediting Karadzic for the situation in Foca. This event was about celebrating the success of Foca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The visit of Karadzic with his wife and the director of the University of Serb Sarajevo, Professor Maksimovic, and the visit to the hospital - and at the time I was director of the hospital, as I am to this day - and then there is my own statement. I stated that because I was a student of the University of Sarajevo Medical School and already in the beginning of 1993 we charted a strategy, to open two faculties in Foca. The University of Serb Sarajevo did not operate before that, and I pointed out that these should be the first two faculties of that university because with academicians Starevic and Olga Blagojevic -- well, the three of us are the people who were in charge of that and to this -- and today we have this university. I have to be quite frank. Although I'm 60 years young, I really cannot say who said what then but I can speak on my own behalf and say what I said then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes. And this -- the only question I had was whether this was a celebration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was a regular visit. It was the first time that Dr. Karadzic visited the hospital with his wife. I remember that as director of the hospital I went out to welcome President Karadzic together with my colleagues in front of the reception area. It was no celebration. What do you mean "celebration"?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I think that we can leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go back and talk with you about Dr. Berberkic who you discussed during cross-examination at transcript page 27558 through 27559. You said that Dr. Berberkic left without permission. What was he doing at the hospital before he left the first time without permission?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Amir Berberkic is a doctor who specialised in surgery. He assisted during our operations and this was training for his further work. Of his own free will he left the operating rooms in the hospital. Now, please don't take my word for it. Seven days, ten days, later he was brought in by persons in uniform, Serb persons, they brought him in as a wounded person and I performed surgery on him. There were old wounds on him. It wasn't within six hours. Afterwards, he was exchanged. I think that he lives in America with his family as far as I know and he did visit Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have some clarification. The transcript indicates that you said afterwards he was exchanged, but my colleagues say that they believe -- that they believe you said he was released. Which of the two is accurate in describing what happened to him afterwards before he ended up in America?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Usually we just ask the witness to repeat himself because there was a -- a confusion somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was discharged from the hospital, but I really could not claim anything now because exchanges did start, official exchanges. According to the International Red Cross, I think that he was in one of these groups that were exchanged, so I infer that; but I don't have exact information so that I could claim either one or the other at the moment. But my conclusion is that he is alive and healthy with his family in America.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said that he was brought in as a wounded man by persons in uniform. Did the -- when he was presented to you for surgery, were there any notations on his medical chart regarding whom to contact after the patient was treated?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a rule. When such patients are brought in, then the rule was that it would be announced when they would be discharged as having been cured. So they were supposed to go home or report to whoever, the police, that took him then as a prisoner of war. So that's why I still stand by what I said, that he was exchanged, because POWs were exchanged later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to another topic, Dr. Torlak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe just before you do. You say "POWs." Was he a POW?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was brought in as a wounded person. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That doesn't make him a POW, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was brought in and he surgery performed on him -- oh, well, then I do apologise. I mean, for me he was a wounded person, he was operated on, he was treated, cured, so I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the explanation. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to Dr. Torlak. You say at transcript page 27556 that he had documents from the authorities. Could you please clarify for us what kind of documents and from what authorities?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably at that time one could not leave the area, probably, that was covered by the local authorities without some papers from the local authorities or the military authorities. I don't know which documents these are, but certainly there had to be document if he was given a car by Dr. Stanic to be taken to Rogatica. I mean, he must have had some kind of valid documents that all people who were leaving the municipality of Foca had to have at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say all people had to have, would that be irrespective of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then what do you mean, "all people who were leaving the municipality had to have at that time"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question. The question is: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as a surgeon, if I were to leave the municipality of Foca for any reason, I had to have documents stating that I was leaving and these documents would also state when I was supposed to come back to my work. If there was a death, for instance, outside Foca, or to take my child or mother somewhere, I mean, I had to have certain papers in addition to a valid ID and everything else. Because I was -- I was duty-bound. I had work obligation. I could not just leave the hospital of my own free will to resolve my own personal problems without having such papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt you there. I understand as a professional you say you had to do that. The question doesn't have to do with professionals or status other than ethnicity. You said no you don't have to be of any ethnic group to have these papers. And what the lawyer is asking you is: If that is not so, then it's not all people? So what do you mean by "all people"? Which are these people, ethnically speaking, who had to have these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean all citizens -- and especially we, leaving the hospital, irrespective of ethnicity, I mean, we are professionals needed by the hospital so that it could function. We are not in hospital because of ethnicity. All of us who were at the hospital were duty-bound to carry out the work that we happened to be doing at the time. Like Dr. Torlak, to visit his family in Rogatica, he had to have papers stating that he could go there to see them and also these papers stated when he was supposed to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Going back to Dr. Berberkic. Did Dr. Berberkic seek such authorisation to leave the hospital and leave his duty post as a doctor for whatever reason, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Ms. Harbour about wounded Muslim women and children that were treated at Foca hospital. Do you have knowledge of any incidents in Foca where Serb women and children were shot, wounded, and/or killed during 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Foca at the 19th of December, 1992, in the area of Osanica, 56 civilians were killed, civilians and soldiers, belonging to three generations aged 3 to 90. The following day in a field 42 Serb civilians and soldiers were killed. And in 1992 at Poljici 20 persons were killed. And in July 40 civilians in the area of Jabuka. These were crimes that affected 100 persons per day within two days. The Foca hospital took care of 2.500 persons, civilians and soldiers. Since there isn't a mortuary in the city - it is the hospital that handled all of that - 650 dead citizens of Foca were taken care of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the last part of the cross-examination you were shown a speech which involved even some words of President Karadzic where he was quoted as saying: "The Muslim republic has given up on Foca ..." What did you understand those words to mean in the context of events in Foca? What had been announced by Muslim authorities for Foca prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are two questions there or more than one at least. Can we split them?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's go with what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What did you understand the words uttered by Mr. Karadzic - "the Muslim republic has given up on Foca" - to mean?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably some divisions, that Foca would not be part of the other entity. That was my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now my second question: What had been announced by Muslim authorities for Foca before the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Foca is a geographical area that is between Sarajevo and Sandzak. Before 1992, there were pre-election activities, big gatherings of the Muslim people from all parts of the former Yugoslavia. There would be 100.000 persons attending these gatherings. So Foca was probably a place that was of interest. I don't know how come. Probably in these global terms, this global planning and everything else in terms of its geographical structure, and that gave rise to tensions and fear among all the citizens of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I thank you for your time both yesterday and today. On behalf of my client and the rest of the team I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness. Just I would like to tender 65 ter 31518B, which was the series of speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, isn't it correct that most of that was read into the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and the witness confirmed that he was present at that event and that he indeed said some of the words that were read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This -- and I asked if it is really necessary to have it in evidence because everything you put to the witness was read into the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but I did not read the entire speech; it would have taken too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I forget, did we have a translation of that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Its up to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. 65 ter 31518B is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6868, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then, Your Honours, the only remaining issue is the associated exhibits, there were three of them, which I would again re-tender at this time given their use in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are these the long list of names?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One is and the other two are shorter I think two-page and one-page --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: There's two long lists and one short one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we defer this decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Doctor, thank you so much for coming to the Tribunal to testify. This brings us to the end of your testimony at the Tribunal. You may now leave. Please travel well back home. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we call the next witness, let me just make some corrigenda items. Now, there is a Rule 92 ter statement for Nedjo Vlaski. On the 14th of October, 2014, in its response to the Defence's Rule 92 ter motion for Witness Vlaski, the Prosecution opposed 52 paragraphs of the witness's statement. The Prosecution stated it opposes these paragraphs as they primarily discuss matters that occurred prior to September 1991 and that the statement gives information with an unclear foundation of the witness's personal knowledge. The Chamber acknowledges that it has previously admitted statements containing certain contextual pre-indictment information as well as unsourced opinions. Having reviewed the statement of Witness Vlaski, the Chamber is however concerned with the high amount of pre-indictment information and unsourced opinion evidence, almost exceeding the amount of factual evidence specifically connected to the indictment. The Chamber therefore instructs the Defence to seriously consider redacting the statement before tendering it into court. And then I also want to deal with the associates exhibits of the same witness. The Chamber notes that on the 21st of October, 2014, the Defence filed a motion to tender 11 exhibits associated with the Rule 92 ter statement of Witness Nedjo Vlaski. The Chamber notes that the document bearing 65 ter 1D05124 is missing the correct English translation. The Chamber invites the Defence to consider reducing the number of associated exhibits by, for example, tendering some of these documents with the witness during examination-in-chief. Maybe I might as well deal with the last item while we have the time, verification of translation procedure. During the testimony of Ratko Adzic, document P6695 was MFI'd due to a translation issue. Through an informal communication the Defence stated that it found errors in the translation. The Chamber hereby advises the Defence to follow the normal procedure for requesting a verification of translations of documents from CLSS and report back once revised translation is received. That concludes that. Mr. Lukic, is the Defence ready to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and my colleague Stojanovic will lead the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. I see Mr. -- both counsel on this side are standing. I will give the lady preference. Yes, Madam Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With your indulgence I would like to be excused from court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are most excused. You are very much excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I have one preliminary matter related to the next witness, and I wonder if we might briefly move into private session for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I hadn't realised he was being brought in. I can address it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It relates to cross-examination, so we need not interrupt him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Good morning, Mr. Vlaski, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, my family name is Djuric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Djuric. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you testify you are expected to make a declaration that you will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else by the truth, a copy of you which has been given to you. Can you please read that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Djuric, you will first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic who is counsel for the Defence of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please tell us your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Mane Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you give a statement to the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to call up 65 ter 1D01730.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the left-hand side of your screen you will see -- or rather, you already see a statement with a signature. Looking at the page, could you please tell us whether the personal information is about you and whether the signature is yours?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the signature?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: The signature is also mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you see a signature. Is it yours and did you also enter the date in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature and I entered the date myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you this: When you were proofed for this testimony, did you indicate a typo in paragraph 48 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at paragraph 48 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 48 a typo has been made which needs to be corrected. The date of the document should not be the 21st of May, 1992, but the 30th [as interpreted] of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Correct. This is a typo. Not the 21st of May, 1992, but the 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify. The question was about a possible date of the 30th and the witness answered the 31st of May. Is that correct, 31st of May, 1992? Witness, I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to indicate that on page 47, line 6 of the record, it says "30th" of May" and I said the "31st of May." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now that we have made a correction in the statement, Mr. Djuric, if I were to put the same questions to you today after you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, would you adhere to your statement in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MANE DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would adhere to my statement in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender the witness's statement into evidence. The document number is 65 ter 1D01730.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The statement is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit D732.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I would also like to tender three associated documents: 1D -- 65 ter 1D02341, 1D02690, and 1D02733.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No objections as to 65 ter 1D02341. The other two were the subject of a correction in a proofing note as to what document should be in what paragraph. And just to make a link with the statement, for the record, I'd request that some kind of record be laid as to what they actually relate to, either the proofing note be tendered or something else be done so that we can connect them in the record to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I see you nodding and raising a hand. Could you say that in words?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours. If the Prosecutor did not have any objections, we could admit them immediately. But if there are objections, I will put my questions, I will -- may establish a link with paragraph 53 as I have previously informed the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, my understanding of the Prosecution is not that they oppose the admission, but they say can you clarify certain issues because there are paragraphs that need explanation and are you -- are you in a position to do that? Do you understand what their concern is and are you able to attend to that so that by the time we admit the documents that problem has been attended to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do it briefly. Let's look at paragraph 53 of the statement, which has been admitted under D732.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there. Can we finish with the admission or nonadmission of exhibits before you go to paragraph 53 of the statement? Has he explained that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the witness's statement there is reference to 1D13031, which supports one part of the witness's statement relative to the setting up of the Patriotic League and the policy pursued by the SDA with regard to the admission and training of police officers.
